slides.text:
Scope is where a name can be used. Every variable lives in a block, and this module shows how far it reaches, how a new variable can hide another with the same name, and which variables live for the whole file.

Three sessions: blocks, shadowing, then the package level and the setup of `if`, `switch` and `for`.

A **block** is the code between a pair of braces: a function, an `if`, a loop, a `case` or braces on their own. A variable lives from its declaration to the closing brace of its block.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
open a block
    make a box
    use the box        ok
close the block
use the box            error

slides.text: A block sees what its outer blocks declared, never the other way around. Two blocks next to each other do not see each other, so each can use the same name.

exercises.title: A block of its own
exercises.guide: Open a block with a pair of braces and declare a variable inside it.

chunks.guide: Declared in `main`, `level` lives until the closing brace of `main`.
Braces alone make a **block**. `bonus` exists only inside it, but the block can still see `level`.

notes.text: A bare block: it opens a new scope.

chunks.guide: Here only `level` is left.

exercises.title: Variables inside an if
exercises.guide: Declare a variable inside each branch of an if.

chunks.guide: A value to test.
Every branch is its own block, so both can declare `grade`: they are two separate variables.

notes.text: A separate variable, in the else branch.

chunks.guide: `grade` is gone here, `score` is not.

exercises.title: What is still there?
exercises.guide: Print the one variable that still exists after the `if`.

exercises.title: Variables in a loop
exercises.guide: Declare a variable inside a loop body and keep a result outside it.

chunks.guide: Declared before the loop, so it survives it.
`square` is a new variable on every lap. `last = square` assigns to the outer one.

notes.text: Created again at the start of every lap.

chunks.guide: The loop is over: `i` and `square` are gone, `last` holds the final value.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.explanation: `total` is declared inside the body, so every lap starts a new one at 0. Nothing carries over between laps.

exercises.title: Each case is a block
exercises.guide: Declare a variable inside two different cases.

chunks.guide: The value the switch looks at.
Each `case` is its own block, like the branches of an `if`: the two `name` variables never meet.

notes.text: A separate variable, in the other case.

chunks.text:
switch day {
    case 1:
        name := "Mon"
        fmt.Println(name)
    case 2:
        name := "Tue"
        fmt.Println(name)
    }

chunks.guide: Only `day` is visible after the switch.

slides.text:
Inside a block, `:=` always makes a new variable, even when the name already exists outside. The new one **shadows** the outer one until the block ends, and the outer one keeps its value.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
outer x = 1
open a block
    new x = 2    hides the outer
close the block
x is 1 again

slides.text:
`=` makes nothing: it changes the variable that already exists. Mixing them up is the classic scope bug: write `:=` where `=` was meant and the outer variable never changes.

A new variable exists only after its own line, so its right side still reads the outer one.

exercises.title: Hide a variable
exercises.guide: Declare a variable with the same name inside a block.

chunks.guide: The outer variable.
`:=` inside the block creates a **new** `x` that hides the outer one until the block ends.

notes.text: A new variable, not a change to the old one.

chunks.guide: The block is over. The outer `x` was never touched.

exercises.title: Change the outer one
exercises.guide: Change the outer variable from inside a block.

chunks.guide: The outer variable.
Without the colon, `=` finds the existing `balance` and changes it.

notes.text: No new variable: this is the outer one.

chunks.guide: The change outlives the block.

exercises.title: Keep the result
exercises.guide: Store the last `i` whose square is above 10 in the `found` declared before the loop.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Pick the output. Watch the colon.
exercises.explanation: `total := total + i` makes a new `total` on every lap, built from the outer one, which stays 0. After the loop the outer `total` is still 0.

exercises.title: All new in a block
exercises.guide: Mix a new and an existing variable in a block.

chunks.guide: Two outer variables.
In a new block, **every** name on the left of `:=` is new, even `host`. Only `port`, with `=`, is the outer one.

notes.text: Both names are new in this block.

chunks.guide: `host` is back to the outer one. `port` was really changed.

exercises.title: What happens when it runs?
exercises.guide: Pick what Go does with this program.
options: It does not compile: the inner count is unused
It does not compile: count is declared twice
exercises.explanation: The inner `count` is a new variable that nothing reads, and Go rejects unused variables. The outer `count` would not have changed anyway.

slides.text: A variable declared outside every function is visible in the whole file, in any order, and from every block. A local variable with the same name hides it, as any other shadowing.

The setup of an `if`, a `switch` or a `for` is a small block around the whole statement. The variable lives in every branch and is gone after the closing brace.

A variable declared before a `for` is not part of that block, so the loop can use it with `=` and it lives on.

exercises.title: Declared after main
exercises.guide: Use a package-level variable that is written below `main`.

chunks.guide: `counter` is not declared yet in this file. That is fine.
A package-level variable is visible inside every block, and the changes stay.
The loop changed the package-level variable.
Package-level names can be declared in any order, even below the code that uses them.

exercises.title: A local hides the package one
exercises.guide: Hide a package-level variable inside a block.

chunks.guide: A package-level variable.
Here `level` is the package one.
The local `level` hides the package one inside the block, the same as shadowing a local.
The package-level variable was never changed.

exercises.title: One variable per branch
exercises.guide: Declare a variable in the setup of an `if` and another in an `else if`.

chunks.guide: A variable from the setup lives in the whole chain: later branches still see `n`, and `m` is seen by what follows it.

notes.text: Can read n from the first setup.

exercises.title: Use the setup variable
exercises.guide: Use the variable of the setup in the condition.

exercises.title: Hide it in a switch
exercises.guide: Hide an outer variable with the setup of a switch.

chunks.guide: The outer variable.
The setup makes a new `n` for the whole switch. It is built from the outer `n`, and then hides it.

notes.text: New variable, built from the old one.

chunks.guide: The switch is over and the outer `n` is back.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Pick the output. Look where `i` is declared.
exercises.explanation: `i` is declared before the loop and the loop only assigns it with `=`, so it survives. The loop stops when `i` reaches 4.
